02

Lizzo — Good As Hell

Directed by Alan Ferguson, set at Southern University in Baton Rouge, Louisiana — reflecting Lizzo's own marching-band background on piccolo and flute. Watch the video

9 Dec 2019
Set video premiered on YouTube (song: 2016, Coconut Oil EP)
Alan Ferguson
Director · Southern University, Baton Rouge setting
3 heroes
Nicole, the break-up and the isolated drummer — narrative within performance
2020 noms
MTV Best Editing · Soul Train Video of the Year · Billboard Top R&B Song

Spot the detail — media language

SettingSouthern University: the practice room, the field and the custom "Lizzo" school bus. The iconography is music, not sport — rows of brass instruments create the triumphant, celebratory mood.
Colour paletteRicher as the narrative progresses: regulation navy tracksuits in practice → bright blue and gold at the homecoming game. Gold connotes glamour and success — and reflects Lizzo's star persona.
CostumeLizzo wears sports kit as "conductor", her own marching-band uniform on the bus, then a dance costume with the Dancing Dolls — always part of the group: unity, support, teamwork.
The three heroes (Propp)Nicole told off in chemistry for loving music; a romantic break-up; a drummer isolated from the percussion section. Each is a Proppian hero helped by other women (and Lizzo) toward the self-love in the lyrics — narrative blended into a performance video.
Technical codesFrequent wide shots of students playing together and marching in formation represent teamwork; Todorov's stages play out from disruption (each problem) to a joyous new equilibrium at the game.
Editing flourishThe trumpet zoom becomes an action match — the bus party appears to be "inside" the trumpet via the matching golden colour scheme. Diegetic sound bookends the video (the "out-take" cheering ending = inclusion and realism).

Representation — reinforcing AND challenging

  • Challenging: Lizzo presents an alternative female body type with pride — eating Cheetos on the bus rejects the stereotype of appearance-first eating; the video explores pressures on young women and Black self-confidence.
  • Reinforcing (arguably): costumes, hair and make-up adhere to female stereotypes — but a post-feminist reading says these construct empowerment through body confidence.
  • Ethnicity: Black male students appear in band uniforms in the locker room — where stereotype would expect sports kit; though the rowdy bus scenes could be read as adhering to a negative stereotype.
  • Direct address from Lizzo builds intimacy with a female audience who relate through personal identity.
Lizzo happily eating Cheetos — rejecting appearance-first food stereotypes
Glamorous costumes, hair and make-up on the Dancing Dolls
Black male students shown in band uniforms rather than sports kit
A large group of Black teenagers being rowdy on a bus in a public space
Nicole admonished in class — the male teacher's authority sets up her arc
The resolution: collective joy — female solidarity as the engine of the narrative

Justin Bieber ft. Quavo — Intentions

Released 7 February 2020, directed by Michael D Ratner — a documentary-style video made with Alexandria House, an LA non-profit supporting women and children out of homelessness. Watch the video

7 Feb 2020
Released, from the album Changes; teased on Twitter the day before
$10,000+
Raised for Alexandria House in the first three days
32m views
First week of Ratner's Bieber docuseries "Seasons" — a YouTube Originals record (where the song title was first revealed: digital convergence)
#32 of 2020
Billboard's songs of the year · MTV Best Pop Video nomination

Spot the detail — media language

TypographyThe graffiti-style title connotes the rap/hip-hop genre and reinforces the urban LA setting.
BahriEstablished through setting, gesture and props: studying, waiting for the bus, working on the long night journey home — her "intention" to study and help others, and the struggle behind it.
MarcyShown in the library — access to education as the way out of challenging circumstances. Her mirror scene cuts both ways: appearance stereotype OR the insecurity many young women feel "representing" themselves to the world.
AngelaOn the streets supporting homeless people in LA — the video's third hero, gifted studio air-time to amplify her work.
The artists as helpersBieber and Quavo are Propp's helpers, not heroes — gifting a car, backpacks of school supplies and studio time. Bieber's red-hoodie direct address and Quavo rapping centre-frame still mark their star power.
Dance — unconventionallySpontaneous, communal dancing (a child on a table, Bahri with friends in the street) conveys shared joy — challenging the choreographed dance convention and reflecting the documentary style.
Gesture codesHugs, smiles, high-fives, hands on shoulders: emotional support, love and community at Alexandria House. The gift moments include tears and hugs — demanding an emotional audience response.
The endingA posed "family" group shot + on-screen "Thank You" reminds us of the video's purpose and represents the ethnically diverse community — with Bieber and Quavo blending in, not standing out.

Representation — and the debate

  • Women of colour: active, not objectified — studying, travelling independently, connecting with others. Empowerment through educational, creative and artistic achievement. Subverts the male gaze — no glamorising, no objectification.
  • Alexandria House: a place of safety, warmth and community (the "welcome" banner, children's artwork) — though representing residents as victims in need arguably reinforces stereotypes, the emphasis is their journey to stability and independence.
  • The artists: represented as caring and generous — part of Bieber's rebrand after earlier negative publicity: mature, compassionate, socially responsible (compare Drake's God's Plan — the same "giving back" cultural moment).
  • The counter-argument: "Don't need a sponsor, nope, you the brand now" — while wearing his own Drew House hoodie: self-promotion undermining the charity? The white saviour question is a legitimate evaluation point.
  • Contexts: social awareness of homelessness, poverty and inequality; women of colour disproportionately affected (BLM-era context); high production values reflect the big-label economics behind the philanthropy.

04

TLC — Waterfalls (1995)

The historical text: the second-biggest girl band of the 90s (after the Spice Girls) tackling drug violence and HIV/AIDS in a cautionary, socially aware video — expressionism, not social realism. Watch the video

Spot the detail — the five key shots

The MCU + pointMedium close-up of the singer directly addressing — and pointing at — the audience: a music video convention that here underlines the cautionary nature of the lyrics and the warning in the video.
The ocean wide shotThe trio perform on water (CGI borrowed from Terminator 2's liquid metal!) — dressed similarly but individually. The water setting links to the lyrics and sets them apart: they are narrators, not characters.
The gang + ghost motherSlightly low angle connotes threat; aggressive gesture codes and frame dominance mean "no escape route". The superimposed mother knows the danger — and couldn't protect her son. Later, the low-angle pavement shot positions us beside his body: sympathy and powerlessness.
The brown paper bagExtreme close-up of a symbolic prop: drugs are never shown — the bag symbolises them, just as AIDS is symbolised by skin deterioration and the montage of the woman's previous partners. Symbolism carries the message.
The romance → horror turnThe HIV/AIDS narrative opens with romance iconography (attractive semi-naked actors, silk, mirrors) — then turns threatening: the over-exposed face and glowing eyes resemble a horror transformation scene.
The opening high angleA bird's-eye view of the city establishes the urban setting — but the camera movement and rapid editing suggest a fall: unsettling, connoting narrative disruption from the very first frames. Inner-city sets (brownstone, stoop, street corner) and costumes (baggy tracksuits, caps, dark glasses) intertextually echo New Jack City and Boyz N The Hood.

Representation

  • The young Black man: NOT a typical gangster — he's trying to make easy money to help his family (the "call me" gesture to his mother shows he cares). He becomes a victim of the violent gang members — who DO reinforce ethnic and gender stereotypes through props, dress and gesture codes.
  • The couple: sexuality first glamorous and intimate; the man's illness is shot in sympathetic close-ups — empathy, not condemnation.
  • TLC themselves: almost supernatural beings manifesting from water. Their image mixes traditionally feminine codes (make-up, colourful crop tops) with masculine ones (loose combat-style trousers hiding their legs — exactly what many hip-hop/R&B videos obsess over). A complex, controlled representation of gender.
  • The overall tone: issues represented sympathetically — a message sent "without preaching".

Context — the 90s on screen

  • Public concern and heavy media coverage of HIV/AIDS (then a deadly condition) and drug-gang street violence — the video's two tragic narratives.
  • Where many R&B videos ran romantic narratives and hip-hop videos celebrated wealth-through-crime, Waterfalls references those conventions but is cautionary, not glamorising.
  • "Gangsta" rappers (Ice-T, NWA, Notorious B.I.G.) also covered poverty and crime, but Waterfalls is more emotional and nuanced than those "ghetto fables".
  • Female solidarity and empowerment — the same message the Spice Girls carried in the mainstream.

Websites & Social Media

You must study each website's homepage design, links to other content, and interactive links to social media. The key concept everywhere: the star persona is a constructed representation, not "the real person".

Music website conventions

House style tied to the latest album — rebranding keeps the star "current"
Star persona constructed through media language
Commercial imperative — singles, tour tickets, merch, store
Interactive features + prominent social media links
Convergent links — out to Spotify, iTunes, ticket sites
Data capture — newsletter sign-ups build a marketing database

Lizzo online

  • Homepage: built around Lizzo as a brand and the latest release — the "Special" era used a black-and-white palette matching the album cover; featured videos, tour dates and official merch combine into one strong commercial message.
  • Menu: Music, Video, Tour, Store — the Store goes to a Warner-run regional site (eurostore.warnermusic.com for the UK): evidence of her major-label machine. Merch: hoodies, tees… and thongs — aimed young.
  • Representation: limited personal identity — a corporate promotional site (an exam judgement: brand first, person second). The wide merch size range (XS–6X, plus Yitty) reflects body-positive culture.
  • Social: pinned tweet promotes the album in house style; Pride support and Juneteenth posts = values-driven persona; venting about fat-shaming = the "real" Lizzo; TikTok is her biggest platform; the same posts appear across platforms (synergy); YouTube is pure marketing; Facebook barely updated — her audience isn't there.
"Special" era homepage: house style = album artwork
The store: commerce via Warner
Twitter: album promo pinned
TikTok: her biggest platform

Justin Bieber online

  • justinbiebermusic.com: sleek, minimal, modern design — the name follows down every page; subtle faded headings; rebranded around each release (the Justice era). Music/Video pages offer stream, download and share for every release; "Load More" reveals years of brand reinvention.
  • Commerce & data: Shop (Drew House adjacent merch), Tour with ticket links, newsletter sign-up; the Photos page is posed and "artistic" — controlled star persona.
  • Social: the businessman (Drew House, the Vespa collaboration framed as gratitude), the loving husband, the relatable dog owner, the topless sex symbol, the charity supporter (therapy organisation for his tour staff), the faith poster — multiple constructed identities for different audience needs.
  • Global strategy: his Asian-market tweets out-perform his English ones; the 2021 Hybe–Ithaca merger (the BTS company merging with his management) connects him to the K-pop machine — industry AND audience evidence.
Justice-era shop: rebrand + commerce
Merch drops
Topless basketball: the sex-symbol persona
The dog post: relatable glimpse of the private world

🔍 Decode the posts — Lizzo

Revision drill: for each real post, say ONE line about what it represents about the artist — then tap to compare. This is exactly the evidence a 20-marker wants.

What does this represent?

Her whole Twitter profile renamed "FOLLOW @YITTY" — a successful businesswoman using her own platform as free advertising for her shapewear brand: synergy in action.

What does this represent?

"My mission is to help as many marginalized people as I can with my platform" — the Big Grrrls casting call shows empowerment and inclusion… and a savvy TV businesswoman (the show is made with Amazon Studios).

What does this represent?

"LET ME TELL U HOW FINE I LOOKED LAST NIGHT" — unapologetic self-love and body confidence: the persona practises exactly what Good As Hell preaches.

What does this represent?

"Everything I do is for HER… so that she grows up knowing how to love herself radically" — a role model for young Black girls; self-love as a mission and a warm, personal fan connection.

What does this represent?

Speaking on anti-Black rhetoric — an activist using her reach to advocate for Black women: the values-driven side of the persona.

What does this represent?

Dancing by the Rolls-Royce — "IM POSTING THIS CUS I FEEL LIKE IT": success and confidence on her own terms, celebrating her body and her wealth without apology.

What does this represent?

Green-screen comedy content — funny and relatable: the "best-friend" persona that makes her TikTok-native and approachable.

What does this represent?

26.9M followers, 1.1B likes — the stat that proves TikTok is her biggest platform; the bio ("100% that bitch | C-E-H-O of @YITTY") mixes the humour with the business empire.

🔍 Decode the posts — Justin Bieber

What does this represent?

Best Pop Act winner, with thanks to fans — the successful, award-winning artist who publicly credits his audience.

What does this represent?

Drew House bears — the successful businessman promoting his own fashion brand to millions of followers, for free.

What does this represent?

"I got the opportunity to design a Vespa" — a synergy deal framed as gratitude: both brands win, and his empire extends beyond music.

What does this represent?

The Tim Hortons "Timbiebs" partnership — synergy with a Canadian icon; the humble hometown-boy persona literally sells doughnuts.

What does this represent?

Free therapy for fans and tour family — caring, humble and mental-health aware: the heart of the mature rebrand (and, critics note, it also tells us what a great guy he is).

What does this represent?

Auctioning a Vegas trip and meet-and-greet for Haiti earthquake relief — the generous philanthropist… via a competition that also drives engagement.

What does this represent?

"My wittle bum bum" with Hailey — the loving husband: family values, intimacy and relatability.

What does this represent?

Tour life by private jet — wealth, success and superstar scale: aspirational content for fans.

What does this represent?

"Go for the Gold, Ladies!!!!!" to @HockeyCanada — the proud, patriotic Canadian and relatable sports fan, supporting women's sport.

What does this represent?

Retweeting Weverse Con (the K-pop platform) — courting the Asian market after the Hybe–Ithaca merger: audience strategy made visible.

Why the # and the links matter (industry vs audience)

  • Industry benefit: hashtags and share buttons are free marketing — audiences retweet and spread the campaign by word of mouth; social managers monitor engagement data to shape the next campaign.
  • Audience benefit: using the # makes fans part of the collective identity of the fandom — building their own online identity through liking and sharing.
  • Artists rarely write all their own posts — brand managers balance promotional and "personal" content; posts can be scheduled across all platforms at once.

06

Industry & Audience

Who owns whom, how the money works, who regulates music videos — and who actually watches.

The industry picture

  • Britain's music industry is the third largest in the world. Streaming (Spotify etc.) now accounts for over 50% of consumption — funded by ads and subscriptions, paying the label per stream — while vinyl revives on nostalgia and collectability.
  • The label process: an advance to the artist → production (recording, mixing, formats) → distribution & circulation (marketing, press, promotion — the single and its music video are marketing tools) → radio/TV plugging, online and social teams, sales to retailers.
  • The Big Three — Universal, Sony and Warner — dominate the global market between them.
  • Lizzo: Atlantic Records → Warner Music Group (→ Access Industries). Bieber: Def Jam → Universal Music Group. Both = subsidiaries of conglomerates: £1m+ video budgets, global promotion, cross-media convergence and synergy.
  • Curran & Seaton: media controlled by a small number of companies driven by profit and power — concentration limits variety, creativity and quality. Drop this theory in any industry answer.
Lizzo: Atlantic → Warner
Bieber: Def Jam → Universal

Regulation — the odd one out

  • Music has no single regulator — a favourite 1-mark trap!
  • The BPI's Parental Advisory scheme is voluntary: the logo flags strong language, violence, sexual/discriminatory/dangerous behaviour on CDs and next to online tracks and videos.
  • The Video Recordings Act 1984 (amended 2014): music DVDs must now be BBFC-classified if they'd be rated 12 or above.
  • Since 2015, the BBFC + YouTube/Vevo age-rate online music videos from Sony, Universal and Warner's UK labels (e.g. Ariana Grande's "Dangerous Woman" got a 15).

Bieber's industry story

  • Discovered on YouTube; signed to Island Def Jam at 14 (2008) after meeting Usher; "Baby" (2010) broke him; five Billboard number-one albums by 19 — the youngest ever.
  • Intentions' director also made the Seasons docuseries — cross-platform promotion; the Hybe–Ithaca merger and his Asian tours show the global industry at work.

Audiences — who and why

  • Lizzo: core 12–25, female-leaning but broad; body-positivity and empowerment values; reached through TikTok-first social strategy and "Merch" slang.
  • Bieber: 69.3M YouTube subscribers — the most-subscribed music artist; "Beliebers" (word of the year shortlists, #Belieber); the teenage-girl audience of 2010 has grown up with him (now ~18–30); hip-hop collabs (Quavo, DJ Khaled, Chance the Rapper) widen the demographic.
  • Psychographics (VALS): mainstreamers (chart radio), aspirers (image-led, Instagram), explorers (live music, new bands), reformers (independent labels only), succeeders (music to unwind).
  • Fandom = active audiences: buying physical/limited editions, memorabilia, merch, dressing the style, concerts, competitions — though streaming's "suggestions" mean the industry still steers what we hear.

Theory applied — ready-made answers

  • Hall's readings of Good As Hell: body-positivity activists = preferred (alternative body type shown with pride); feminists = negotiated (love the independence; question the make-up and revealing outfits); some men = oppositional (reject the negative male characters — the coach, the ex).
  • Hall on Intentions: a woman who has experienced sheltered housing might read it negotiated — valuing the awareness, triggered by the memories.
  • U&G (PIES): personal identity (a long-commute student sees herself in Bahri; women relate to Lizzo's confidence) · information (the videos raise awareness of homelessness; websites carry tour news) · entertainment (feel-good dance and celebration) · social interaction (fan comments, sharing, the fandom itself).
  • The debate in Intentions: are we positioned as an active audience (donate, get involved) or passive consumers of Bieber's rebrand? Both sides earn marks.

07

Exam-Style Practice

Music questions are essay-led: 20-mark statement questions comparing the two modern videos, plus context and online-media questions. Always: specific examples, media terminology, judgements and conclusions.

Q1 · "'Music videos reinforce gender stereotypes.' How far is this true of Good As Hell?" [20-style]

Explore gender representations · refer to contexts (social/cultural) · agree AND disagree, then judge.

Reinforces: costumes, hair and make-up on the Dancing Dolls adhere to female stereotypes; men hold authority roles (the coach, the ex). Challenges: Lizzo's alternative body type shown with pride (context: the rise of body positivity); the Cheetos moment; women drive every narrative and rescue each other — female solidarity as the engine. The post-feminist judgement: the same glamour can be read as empowerment through body confidence — so the video both uses and subverts stereotypes, and your conclusion should say HOW FAR each way.

Q2 · "'Music videos reinforce stereotypes of ethnicity.' How far is this true of the two music videos you have studied?" [20]

Intentions: largely challenges — women of colour active, educated and empowered, not objectified (subverting the male gaze); the diverse "family" ending; Alexandria House as warm community. But the white-saviour critique and victim framing complicate it. Good As Hell: Black excellence at an HBCU — band uniforms where stereotype expects sports kit; celebration and self-confidence; though the rowdy bus scene could be read as adhering to a negative stereotype. Contexts: BLM-era representation, body positivity, the "giving back" celebrity culture. Conclusion: both videos mostly challenge, with specific moments you can argue either way.

Q3 · "How do music videos reflect the time in which they were made? Refer to TLC to support your points." [10]

Waterfalls reflects mid-90s public concern over HIV/AIDS (then deadly — symbolised through the man's deteriorating skin and the photo montage) and drug-gang violence (the brown-bag symbol, the son's murder). Its inner-city mise-en-scène and costume intertextually reference 90s films like New Jack City and Boyz N The Hood; its water CGI shows off Terminator 2-era technology. As "socially aware" hip-hop, it reflects a moment when gangsta rap dominated but TLC chose the cautionary, sympathetic route — female solidarity in the era of the Spice Girls.

Q4 · "How far are these two artists able to represent themselves through social media?" [20]

They can: Lizzo vents about fat-shaming abuse and posts her values (Pride, Juneteenth) — the "real" person breaking through; Bieber constructs multiple selves (husband, businessman, believer, joker). But: both personas are managed — brand managers balance promotional and personal posts, house styles are locked to album campaigns, and the same content is syndicated across platforms; Lizzo's Facebook is barely hers, Bieber's posts sell Drew House and Vespa. Judgement: social media offers a *curated* authenticity — more self-representation than a website allows, but still shaped by the commercial machine (Curran & Seaton).
